lines: A team reading a Debezium topic simplifies it for whatever sink is downstream, keeping only the actual column values each record carries.
The field that named what kind of change each record actually was goes along with everything else that gets stripped away.
From that point on, a row that just finished catching up during a fresh snapshot looks exactly the same as a row that was genuinely just inserted.
Before I show you what that simplified record actually looks like, think through this with me.
Once a record has been stripped down to just its own column values, with nothing else attached.
Can whatever reads that record still tell a snapshot catching up apart from a brand-new row actually being inserted?
answer: The column values by themselves carry no memory of how that row came to exist in the first place.
Both cases now look identical, because the one field that ever distinguished them is exactly the field that got thrown away.

lines: Here's something worth knowing before looking at a single field of any event.
This capture tool can actually run in three genuinely different shapes, not just one.
It can run as a connector inside a shared cluster, as its own standalone application with no cluster at all, or as a plain library embedded directly inside somebody's own code.
I confirmed the shape of a full event directly, against a real decoded change from this sandbox's own database.
A freshly inserted row carried nothing at all in the slot meant for what the row looked like beforehand, since there was no before state to carry.
An updated row carried real values in both the before slot and the after slot, exactly as the full card promises.
Now here's exactly what gets thrown away when a team simplifies that full card.
The simplifying step keeps only the after values and throws the entire rest of the card away by default.
So the row's own earlier state, what kind of change it was, and where it came from are all gone unless a team explicitly configures the step to keep them.
I measured that simplifying step directly, against a real card built from this sandbox's own database.
Simplifying a real update left behind nothing but its column values, with no trace of where it came from or what kind of change it was.
A real deleted row, simplified the same way, didn't disappear outright — it came through as its last known values plus a flag marking it as gone.
Here's the one setting that actually decides whether a sink can safely see the same event twice.
Telling the sink to either update an existing row or insert a brand-new one, depending on whether that row's key already exists, is what makes its writes safe to repeat.
With that setting on, sending the exact same event through a second time leaves the destination table in exactly the state it was already in.
I put that exact claim to the test, against a real sink table in the real database.
I sent one simplified record through to that table, then sent the identical record through again right afterward.
The row ended up in the exact same state after both attempts, and the table never grew a second row out of that repeat.
Let's pull together what today actually covered, because four separate pieces fit into one picture.
There are three different shapes this capture tool can run in, one shared card every one of them produces, and a simplifying step that trades fields away for less to carry.
A sink only stays safe to replay because of one specific setting, never automatically, and that's the whole thread running through today.
One more question, because a team might assume every sink behaves the same way by default.
Say a team sets up a sink and never explicitly turns on that update-or-insert setting at all.
Sending one already-applied event through that sink a second time — is the destination table still guaranteed to end up in the same state?
answer: Nothing about a sink is safe to repeat by default — that guarantee only ever came from one specific setting, turned on deliberately.
Without it, sending the same event through twice can easily insert a second, duplicate row instead of correcting the one that's already there.
